extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, IP counsel, and judges dealing with claim construction and indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. § 112
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and practical criteria for determining (1) whether a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. § 112, ¶ 6 (means-plus-function), and (2) whether the specification discloses corresponding structure (including required algorithms for software) sufficient to avoid indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against means-plus-function when 'means' not used
rubrics_metrics.description: If the limitation does not use the term 'means,' it is subject to a rebuttable presumption that it is not in means-plus-function form. Williamson, 792 F.3d at 1348.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption may be overcome if the challenger demonstrates that the claim term fails to recite sufficiently definite structure or else recites function without reciting sufficient structure for performing that function. Courts should explain application of the presumption but need not rely on extrinsic evidence to overcome it; intrinsic evidence alone may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for whether claim words connote structure (Williamson test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine 'whether the words of the claim are understood by persons of ordinary skill in the art to have a sufficiently definite meaning as the name for structure.' Williamson, 792 F.3d at 1349.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to how a person of ordinary skill in the art would understand the term as a name for structure, using intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history). If the term is understood as the name of structure, § 112, ¶ 6 does not apply; if not, it may be means-plus-function.

rubrics_metrics.name: No categorical rule for 'processor' — examine context
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no categorical rule that 'processor' is or is not structural; whether 'processor' connotes structure depends on context and how it is used in the claim and specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If 'processor' is used generically as an equivalent to 'means' (a nonce word), or if the claim/specification does not describe how the processor interacts with other components to impart structure, the presumption against means-plus-function may be overcome. Conversely, conventional code or other structural disclosure could support a structural reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional/self-referential claiming is means-plus-function in essence
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim language that describes only what a component does (e.g., 'configured to manage collaborative applications') without structural detail is self-referential and captures any structures that perform the function — the 'epitome of functional claiming.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such black-box functional descriptions (e.g., 'What manages the collaborative applications? The processor.') indicate lack of structure and support a means-plus-function construction because they sweep broadly to 'any and all structures that fulfill the function.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify function and corresponding structure (§ 112, ¶ 6 step two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a limitation is deemed means-plus-function, the court must (1) identify the claimed function and (2) identify the corresponding structure in the specification that performs that function, and clearly link that structure to the function. Williamson, 792 F.3d at 1351; Triton Tech. of Tex., LLC v. Nintendo of Am., Inc., 753 F.3d 1375, 1378 (Fed. Cir. 2014).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patentee fails to disclose adequate corresponding structure, the claim is indefinite. The specification must disclose structure (not merely restate the function) and must clearly link that structure to the claimed function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of algorithm disclosure for special-purpose computer functions
rubrics_metrics.description: For general-purpose computers or processors performing a claimed function, the specification must disclose an algorithm (a step-by-step procedure for accomplishing a given result) as corresponding structure; mere functional description or lists of data components are insufficient. Alfred E. Mann Found. for Sci. Res. v. Cochlear Corp., 841 F.3d 1334, 1342 (Fed. Cir. 2016).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Databases or lists of components that 'enable storage of data' do not constitute an algorithm. To prevent pure functional claiming, the spec should provide algorithmic detail or conventional code/structure that shows how the function is performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must clearly link disclosed structure to claimed function
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must identify corresponding structure for performing the claimed function and clearly link that structure to the function; bare mention of components without showing how they perform the function is inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court looks for a disclosure that connects structure (e.g., code, modules, algorithms, steps) to the specific claimed function. Mere examples or enabling storage/recording of data do not satisfy the linkage requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Databases or lists of components are not necessarily structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing databases that 'enable storing of data related to collaborative applications' is functional and does not necessarily describe structure for performing 'managing' functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specification passage that only lists databases or components (e.g., 'databases 107, 108, 109 enabling...') without describing how those components carry out the claimed function will likely be insufficient as corresponding structure for §112 ¶6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superficial replacement of 'means' with functional language does not avoid § 112, ¶ 6
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing the term 'means' with other functional language (e.g., 'processor configured to...') does not avoid a means-plus-function construction if the amended claim still fails to recite corresponding structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments during prosecution substituting 'a collaborative application management processor configured to manage collaborative applications' for 'means for management of collaborative applications' do not automatically confer structure; the patentee must recite structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic evidence can suffice; extrinsic evidence not always required
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) can be informative and sufficient to determine whether disputed claim language recites sufficiently definite structure or was intended to invoke §112, ¶ 6; extrinsic evidence (expert testimony) is not always required. Dyfan, 28 F.4th at 1365, Diebold Nixdorf, Inc. v. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 899 F.3d 1291, 1299 (Fed. Cir. 2018).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may construe limitations and find terms structural or functional based on intrinsic record alone; however, conventional code or expert testimony (when present) may support a structural reading in appropriate cases (e.g., Dyfan, Zeroclick).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and quantum of proof for indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: The challenger seeking to invalidate a claim as indefinite for lack of corresponding structure bears the ultimate burden to show indefiniteness by clear and convincing evidence. Budde v. Harley-Davidson, Inc., 250 F.3d 1369, 1376–77; Intel Corp. v. VIA Techs., Inc., 319 F.3d 1357, 1365–66.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts evaluate the intrinsic record and any extrinsic evidence under the clear-and-convincing standard when determining whether the specification discloses adequate corresponding structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for claim construction and indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction determinations (including whether claim language invokes §112, ¶ 6) and indefiniteness determinations are legal questions reviewed de novo on appeal (with underlying factual determinations subject to review as appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Teva Pharm. USA, Inc. v. Sandoz, Inc., 574 U.S. 318 (2015) for distinction between underlying factual findings and ultimate legal interpretation; appellate courts review these legal conclusions de novo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of how claimed component interacts with other components
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation that fails to describe how a claimed module interacts with other components (i.e., lacks interaction/structural detail) is less likely to be understood as structural and more likely to be treated as functional/means-plus-function. Williamson, 792 F.3d at 1351.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for claim/spec language that describes interactions or connections among components that would impart structural character; absence of such interactions supports finding of functional claiming.
